passages.happening:
Paul gives Timothy his most solemn charge. “I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His appearing and His kingdom: Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction” (verses 1-2).

He says why. “For the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires. So they will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths” (verses 3-4).

“But you, be sober in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Paul speaks as if they were standing in a courtroom, with God and Christ Jesus as witnesses. The one who ‘will judge the living and the dead’ is watching. That is how serious this charge is.

‘Preach the word.’ The word is the message of the gospel. Timothy is to announce it, the way a herald announced a king's news in the town square. ‘In season and out of season’ means when it is welcome and when it is not, when it is convenient and when it is not.

The three verbs cover what preaching does. ‘Reprove’ shows someone where they are wrong. ‘Rebuke’ warns them to stop. ‘Encourage’ comes alongside to help. And all three are to be done ‘with every form of patient instruction’. Patience and teaching hold the hard words in place.

Then comes a picture: ‘itching ears’. Some people want their ears scratched. They gather teachers who tell them what they already want to hear, and they leave the truth for stories that please them.

That is a warning for every listener, and for every teacher too. It is easy to be a teacher who scratches itching ears. Paul tells Timothy to be ‘sober’, clear-headed and steady, to endure hard things, and to work as an evangelist, telling the good news to people who have not yet believed it.
passages.ot:
God gave his prophets the same kind of charge. To Ezekiel he said, “As for you, O son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; so hear the word from My mouth and give them the warning from Me” (Ezekiel 33:7).

Isaiah knew the itching ear. The people “say to the seers, ‘Stop seeing visions!’ and to the prophets, ‘Do not prophesy to us the truth! Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions” (Isaiah 30:10). And Jeremiah lamented, “The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority. My people love it so” (Jeremiah 5:31).

The coming Judge is in the psalms too: “He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness” (Psalm 96:13).
passages.asks: Paul warns of itching ears. Ask whether you look for teaching that tells you what you already want to hear. Ask whether you are willing to be corrected by God's word, and not only comforted by it. And ask who around you has not yet heard the good news, and how you might tell it, patiently, in season and out.

passages.t: Poured out: the fight, the race, the crown
passages.happening:
Paul speaks of his own death. “For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (verses 6-7).

“From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Paul expects the court to condemn him. He uses two pictures for his death, and neither is grim.

The first is a drink offering. In Israel's worship, wine was poured out at the altar with the sacrifices. Paul had used the same picture years before (Philippians 2:17). Now he says it is happening: ‘I am already being poured out’. His whole life has been given to God, and the last of it is being poured out too.

The second is ‘departure’. The word was used for untying a boat from its moorings, or taking down a tent to move on. For Paul, death is a setting out. In another letter he wrote, “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed” (Philippians 1:23).

Then he looks back. ‘I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.’ These are pictures from the games, the wrestling match and the footrace. He is not boasting. He has kept what was entrusted to him, and he is handing it on.

And he looks ahead. The crown here is the wreath given to a winning athlete. It is ‘laid up’, kept safe. The Lord will give it ‘on that day’, when he appears. And Paul at once refuses to keep it to himself: it is for ‘all who crave His appearing’. Every believer who longs for Christ to come will share it.
passages.ot:
The drink offering came from Israel's sacrifices: with each lamb offered, “you are to prepare a quarter hin of wine as a drink offering” (Numbers 15:5).

The psalms speak tenderly of the death of God's people: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints” (Psalm 116:15). “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me” (Psalm 23:4). And the Teacher says that at death “the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

Daniel saw the end of faithful lives: “those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12:3).
passages.hard:
Paul writes calmly about his own death, even gladly. How should we read words like these, and what about those who are afraid of dying or grieving?

Paul is not wishing to end his own life, and nothing here praises it. He faces a death that others will bring on him, for the sake of the gospel, and he faces it trusting Christ. His calm comes from what he believes: that Christ has broken death's power (1:10), that to depart is to be with Christ, and that the dead will be raised. Christians differ on some details of the time between death and the resurrection, as the doctrine study ‘Death and the Intermediate State’ sets out, but all confess that those who belong to Christ are his in death and will rise.

Nor do these verses ask anyone to be calm on demand. The Bible calls death an enemy, and Jesus wept at a grave (John 11:35). Fear of dying is human, and grief for someone who has died is love going on.

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul could say he had kept the faith. Ask what you would want to be able to say at the end of your own life, and what would need to change now for you to say it. Ask whether you long for Christ's appearing, or rarely think of it. And if someone you love is facing death, ask how you could be with them, as Onesiphorus and Luke were with Paul.

passages.t: Come quickly: who left, who stayed, and what to bring
passages.happening:
“Make every effort to come to me quickly, because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry. Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus” (verses 9-12).

“When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
After the crown comes a list of names, and the list hurts.

Demas had been with Paul in an earlier imprisonment, and Paul had named him as a fellow worker (Philemon 1:24; Colossians 4:14). Now he has gone, ‘in his love of this world’. Paul does not say exactly what that means. It is the opposite of verse 8: Demas loved this present age more than Christ's appearing.

Crescens and Titus have gone too, but Paul says nothing against them. They were probably sent on work. Tychicus Paul sent himself.

‘Only Luke is with me.’ Luke the physician, who wrote the Gospel and Acts, as early Christian writers report, stayed.

Then there is Mark. Years before, Mark had turned back on Paul's first missionary trip, and Paul had refused to take him again, so sharply that he and Barnabas went separate ways (Acts 13:13; 15:37-39). Now Paul asks for him by name: ‘he is useful to me’. The friendship was mended. People change, and Paul let Mark change.

Last, the coat and the books. Sea travel on the Mediterranean mostly stopped in winter, and a Roman prison could be cold and dark. Paul wanted his heavy cloak. He also wanted his scrolls and ‘especially the parchments’, more costly writing material made from animal skin. No one knows what they held: perhaps copies of the Scriptures, perhaps his own notes. Even near death, Paul wanted to read.
passages.ot:
The psalms know the pain of a friend who leaves: “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9). “For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure” (Psalm 55:12).

And they know the God who stays when others go: “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10).

Proverbs values the friend nearby: “Do not forsake your friend or your father’s friend” (Proverbs 27:10).
passages.asks: The list holds a man who left, a man who stayed, and a man who came back. Ask which of them you are most like right now. Ask whether there is someone, like Mark, whom you have written off, and whether God may have changed them. And ask whether there is a lonely person who needs you to bring them something as ordinary as a coat.

passages.t: Alexander; deserted by all, but the Lord stood by me
passages.happening:
“Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message” (verses 14-15).

“At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (verses 16-17).

“And the Lord will rescue me from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom. To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
We do not know exactly what Alexander did. The name was common, and it is not certain he is the Alexander of 1 Timothy 1:20. A coppersmith worked in metal. Paul says he did ‘great harm’ and fought hard against the gospel. Paul warns Timothy to be careful of him.

Then Paul tells of his ‘first defense’, most likely a first hearing in a Roman court. Friends could stand beside an accused man and speak for him. No one did. Everyone stayed away.

Notice what Paul says about those who left him: ‘May it not be charged against them.’ He forgives them, as Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). They failed out of fear, and Paul knew how weak fear can make anyone.

‘But the Lord stood by me.’ When every human friend was gone, Christ was there. And Paul used even that lonely hearing to speak about Jesus, so that the message was proclaimed where Rome's officials could hear it.

‘Delivered from the mouth of the lion’ is a picture, taken from Psalm 22, for being rescued from deadly danger. Roman citizens were not normally thrown to animals. Paul means he was saved, for now, from death.

And for the future? Paul does not expect to escape execution. He expects the Lord to rescue him from ‘every evil action’ and bring him ‘safely into His heavenly kingdom’. Death will not stop that rescue. It will finish it.
passages.ot:
Paul's words about Alexander echo the psalms and Proverbs: “For You will repay each man according to his deeds” (Psalm 62:12), and “Will He not repay a man according to his deeds?” (Proverbs 24:12). The law gives vengeance to God alone: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35). And Proverbs says, “Do not say, ‘I will avenge this evil!’ Wait on the LORD, and He will save you” (Proverbs 20:22).

The lion's mouth comes from the psalm of the suffering one, which Jesus prayed on the cross: “Save me from the mouth of the lion” (Psalm 22:21). And Daniel, rescued from the lions, said, “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions” (Daniel 6:22).
passages.hard:
Paul says of Alexander, ‘The Lord will repay him according to his deeds’, and a moment later prays that those who deserted him will not be held to account. Is that a contradiction? And is Paul wishing harm on Alexander?

The difference lies in what each did. Those who stayed away from Paul's hearing failed out of fear, and he forgives them. Alexander did great harm and fought hard against the message itself. Paul does not take revenge or call for it. He leaves Alexander to God's justice, as he taught in Romans 12:19: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath”. And he warns Timothy to protect himself.

Some readers still feel a tension with Jesus' command to pray for enemies. Many answer that handing an unrepentant opponent over to God's just judgment is not the same as wishing him harm. It is the stance of many psalms, and of the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:10, who leave justice to God. Paul holds both together: mercy for the weak, and trust in God's justice for those who fight against the truth.

These verses do not give anyone leave to curse people they dislike. And if someone has done you great harm, they do not ask you to stay near them or keep silent. Paul warned Timothy to beware. Where a crime has been done, it is right to report it to the authorities. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul forgave friends who failed him, and left an enemy to God. Ask whether there is someone who let you down out of weakness whom you could forgive. Ask whether there is someone who did you real harm whom you need to leave to God, rather than carry the wish for revenge. And ask whether you have known the Lord standing by you when others did not.

passages.happening:
“Greet Prisca and Aquila, as well as the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus has remained at Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus” (verses 19-20).

“Make every effort to come to me before winter. Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers” (verse 21).

“The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Prisca, also called Priscilla, and her husband Aquila had worked beside Paul for years, in Corinth and Ephesus, and had once risked their lives for him (Acts 18; Romans 16:3-4). The household of Onesiphorus is greeted again (see 1:16-18).

Erastus and Trophimus had travelled with Paul (Acts 19:22; 20:4). Notice that Paul left Trophimus sick. The apostle who had seen God heal people did not heal every friend. Sickness came to Paul's circle as it comes to everyone.

‘Come to me before winter.’ If Timothy waited, the sea would close and he might not reach Rome until spring. We are not told whether he came in time.

Four people in Rome send greetings. Of Eubulus, Pudens and Claudia nothing more is known for certain. Irenaeus, in the late second century, names a Linus as the first leader of the church in Rome after the apostles, and takes him to be this Linus. That is early, but it cannot be confirmed.

The last words are a blessing. ‘The Lord be with your spirit’ is for Timothy alone. ‘Grace be with you all’ is plural, for the whole church who would hear the letter read. Paul's last written words, as far as we know, are a prayer for grace.
passages.ot:
‘The Lord be with you’ is an old greeting among God's people. When Boaz came to his fields he said to the workers, “The LORD be with you.” And they answered, “The LORD bless you” (Ruth 2:4).

And the blessing of grace goes back to the priests' blessing over Israel: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:24-25).
passages.asks: Paul's last lines are full of names. Ask who the people are who have worked beside you in faith, and whether you have told them what they mean to you. Ask whether there is someone you should go to ‘before winter’, before it is too late. And hear the last words as spoken to you: the Lord be with your spirit; grace be with you.
